claim_verdicts.evidence: dotnet docs, Threads and threading: "A *process* is an executing program. An operating system uses processes to separate the applications that are being executed." GC fundamentals: "Each process has its own, separate virtual address space." The id half is confirmed by execution on dotnet 10: `dotnet run --project samples/DonHang.Samples -- hello-process` printed "process id: 16180".

"Each process has its own, separate virtual address space." (GC fundamentals) and, for the explicit-sharing half, Memory-Mapped Files: non-persisted files "are suitable for creating shared memory for inter-process communications (IPC)" — cross-process sharing goes through an operating-system facility a program must ask for.

Docker docs on detached mode: "Docker can run your container in detached mode or in the background. To do this, you can use the `--detach` or `-d` for short. Docker starts your container the same as before but this time will \"detach\" from the container and return you to the terminal prompt." Execution: `docker compose ps` on the example repo returned "db running / lab running / web running" long after up.sh had returned, and commands still ran inside that lab box.

Environment.Exit: 'Terminates this process and returns an exit code to the operating system.' main-command-line.md:64: 'your program can send status information to other programs or scripts that run the executable. A return value of 0 usually means success.' exceptions-in-managed-threads.md:15: 'the unhandled exception causes the application to terminate.' Ran in the stage-0 lab box: kill+wait -> 143, kill -9 + wait -> 137, ( exit 3 ) -> 3, undisturbed end -> 0. The 143/137 come from the shell (128+signal), not the OS; and a chosen 'exit 7' is indistinguishable from a crash.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: A process ends on its own (its main function returns, or it asks to end), it crashes, or something outside it asks the operating system to stop it. Whoever started it reads one number for the run: the exit code the program chose, or, when it was stopped from outside, the number the shell that started it reports for that kind of stop.

claim_verdicts.evidence: dotnet docs, Main() return values: "When you return `int` or `Task<int>`, your program can send status information to other programs or scripts that run the executable. A return value of `0` usually means success, and a nonzero value means there's an error." The lesson's hedge ("The convention is") matches the doc's "usually".

Process.Id (net-10.0): "The system-generated unique identifier of the process that is referenced by this Process instance." CA1837 treats `Process.GetCurrentProcess().Id` and `Environment.ProcessId` as the same value: "This rule locates calls to `System.Diagnostics.Process.GetCurrentProcess().Id` and suggests using `System.Environment.ProcessId` instead." Execution on dotnet 10: the sample printed "process id: 16180".

CA1839 describes the property as "getting the path to the file that launched the process". Execution on dotnet 10: `dotnet run ... -- hello-process` printed "started from: ...\\bin\\Debug\\net10.0\\DonHang.Samples.exe" — the executable that was started, not the source file.

Process.Id: property value is 'The system-generated unique identifier of the process'; Remarks: 'Process identifiers can be reused by the system. The Id property value is unique only while the associated process is running.' Two runs of scripts/computer/list-processes.sh in the stage-0 lab box gave pids 1481/1482 then 1499/1500 for the same sleep program. CA1839: Environment.ProcessPath is 'the path to the file that launched the process', i.e. it names the started file, the same file on every run started the same way.

The only programs the script starts are the two `sleep`s on lines 7 and 9, both killed on line 15, plus ps/sed on line 13; nothing is started after line 15.

list-processes.sh line 5 is `[ -f /.dockerenv ] || exec "$(dirname "$0")/../lab-run.sh" "$0" "$@"`, and lab-run.sh line 18 is `exec docker compose exec -T lab bash -c ...`, which can only attach to a running lab service. Executed in the stage-0 lab box (bash 5.3.9(1)-release, x86_64-alpine-linux-musl): a script doing 'sleep 5 &' twice reached the next command 14 ms later, and 'ps -o pid=,args= -p $a,$b' listed both ('1444 sleep 5', '1445 sleep 5') while the script continued. No bash documentation mirror exists under refs/ and versions.yaml pins no shell, so this rests on execution in the pinned lab image only, which is what the claim says.

Same lab box: after 'sleep 5 & a=$!; sleep 5 & b=$!', $! printed 1445 and ps listed 1445 as the second sleep, so $! is that program's id. Running '( exit 3 )' left $! unchanged at 1445; only the next backgrounded command ('( sleep 1 ) &') moved it to 1450. So a subshell that is not backgrounded does not set $!.

Same lab box: 'wait $a' after 'kill $a' returned status 143; 'wait $d' on a sleep that finished normally returned 0. 'wait $b || echo ...' ran the right-hand side and saw 143; '( exit 0 ) && echo' ran, '( exit 0 ) || echo' did not; '( exit 3 ) || echo' ran and saw 3, '( exit 3 ) && echo' did not. The repository script itself prints 'the first one ended with exit code 143', 'a program that succeeds exits with 0' and 'a program that fails exits with 3'.

issues.quote: The `2>/dev/null` on the two `wait` lines only hides a warning message that appears when a program the script started is stopped from outside.
issues.text: False about this code in the stage-0 lab box. Removing ' 2>/dev/null' from both wait lines in scripts/computer/list-processes.sh leaves stdout identical and stderr empty (0 bytes, measured twice). bash 5.3.9 prints no message for a job stopped by the signal plain `kill` sends; a message appears only for signals it reports, e.g. 'kill -9' -> '... 1469 Killed  sleep 30' with wait returning 137. The lesson tells the reader to expect a warning that never appears, and attributes it to 'stopped from outside' in general.
issues.fix: Replace the sentence with: 'The `2>/dev/null` on the two `wait` lines is a precaution: it throws away anything the shell might print about how a stopped program ended. With the stop this script performs, the shell prints nothing, so removing it changes no output.' Or drop the sentence entirely and say nothing about the redirect.

issues.quote: or — when it was stopped from outside — a fixed number the operating system uses to mark that kind of stop
issues.text: Misattributed. The operating system does not hand the starter a number for a stopped process; the shell that started it turns the stop into one (128 + the signal). Measured in the same lab box: plain `kill` -> 143, `kill -9` -> 137, so the number is not 'fixed' for 'that kind of stop' either. The same words recur in section 5, on the 143. Also 'one number that says which ending it was' is too strong on its own: a program that ends by itself can choose to return 143 or 134, so the number alone does not always separate a crash from a chosen failure.
issues.fix: In section 4 write: '... or - when it was stopped from outside - the number the shell that started it reports for that kind of stop, which is fixed for a given way of stopping.' Make the section 5 sentence match ('143 is what the script reports for the first copy after it was stopped from outside: the number the shell reports for that kind of stop'). Keep 0 = success / nonzero = failure as the only thing the number is claimed to say for endings a program chooses itself.
